newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan tries to broker Afghan peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan tries to broker Afghan peace talks.

text.p: Pakistan, trying to regain credibility as an honest broker in Afghanistan, has launched a diplomatic drive to convene an international peace conference.
But Pakistan's efforts have not yet brought any lull in the violence plaguing Afghanistan's war-weary people.
Rival factions launched air raids on each other's cities on Sunday as the Taleban militia battled its foes north of Kabul.
Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan leaves for Moscow on Monday for talks at which the Afghan crisis is expected to feature prominently.

Last month Pakistan announced plans to ask Russia and the United States to act as guarantors of any deal emerging from a proposed conference in Islamabad that would bring together Afghanistan's six neighbours as well as rival Afghan factions.
No date for the conference has been set and it was not clear how it might fit in with separate peace efforts led by United Nations special envoy to Afghanistan, Norbert Holl.
Pakistan launched its initiative after a diplomatic debacle in May when it became the first country formally to recognise the purist Islamic Taleban as Afghanistan's legitimate rulers.

Its triumphal recognition was announced a day after Taleban warriors entered the opposition citadel of Mazar-i-Sharif, thanks to an alliance with General Abdul Malik, who had mutinied against former northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The Taleban victory turned sour within 72 hours as Malik's ethnic Uzbek troops switched sides and linked up with an opposition Shi'ite Moslem militia to drive the bearded fighters from Mazar-i-Sharif in a bloody 15-hour street battle.
Pakistan hastily evacuated its diplomats from its consulate in the northern city, persuading a reluctant Uzbekistan to let them flee to safety across the Friendship Bridge at the border.
The fiasco deepened the gulf between Pakistan and Afghan opposition factions unconvinced by Islamabad's repeated denials that it acts as the Taleban's principal external backer.
On Friday, Malik told Pakistan to withdraw remaining consulate staff from Mazar-i-Sharif, saying popular anger at Pakistan's role meant he could not guarantee their safety.
But Islamabad is pressing ahead with its twin-track bid to persuade Afghan factions and foreign powers to join talks to end the conflict that has torn Afghanistan apart for 18 years.
The Iranian and Uzbek ambassadors to Islamabad last week indicated their countries' willingness to attend.
Russia and the Central Asian states are deeply suspicious of the Taleban as a possible source of Islamic militancy that could spread northwards across Afghanistan's borders.
Iran is also hostile towards the Taleban, saying their harsh religious strictures have brought Islam into disrepute.
While his boss travels to Moscow, a senior Pakistani foreign ministry official, Iftikhar Murshid, was due to go to Taleban headquarters in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar on Tuesday.
Murshid, who held talks with opposition leader Malik in Mazar-i-Sharif last week, expects to return to the northern capital after his talks in Kandahar, newspapers reported.
Murshid is trying to bridge the gap between the Taleban, who want an exchange of prisoners as a precondition for talks, and their opponents, who insist that a ceasefire must come first.
The opposition has demanded that Taleban-controlled Kabul be demilitarised ahead of talks on the formation of a broad-based government -- a goal to which all parties pay lip service.
While willing to receive emissaries, Afghan factions still seem more intent on waging war than talking peace.

Last week the Taleban launched air raids on the northern opposition-held town of Maimana, which Taleban officials said were reprisals for earlier opposition strikes on the Taleban-held city of Kunduz, in northeastern Afghanistan.
Taleban forces are also locked in battle with fighters loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood around the town of Jabal-os-Siraj, 70 km (44 miles) north of Kabul.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press said on Sunday that the Taleban had gained ground in heavy overnight fighting, in which it said they had killed at least 27 opposition fighters and captured 80. Four Taleban were killed and several wounded.
Masood controls the Salang Pass north of Jabal-os-Siraj, as well as his native Panjsher Valley northeast of the town.
The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September, are fighting to impose their strict Islamic rule across Afghanistan.
